When cracking a bunch of eggs, I usually crack them against each other. This is done reliably by denting the side of one egg with the tip of the other. 
The egg's tip is its structurally strongest part, resembling an architectural arch which transfers the energy of the impact evenly across the shell.*
Thus, you have one trusty cracking egg to work you way through your dozens. For me, this is the ideal compromise of working cleanly (not pushing the bacteria-ridden shell into the egg) and efficiently (as the dent may be made more precise than with hitting on a flat surface). 
Also, to me it feels like I have the most control using this egg-on-egg technique. Likely because I can coordinate my hands more accurately in relation to each other than I can one hand and one object (bowl/work surface).

Lastly, I would like to recognize the beauty of going to such depths on matters so seemingly mundane and I truly respect you for this level of dedication in your work.

My experience of doing and observing results over the past couple of years revealed (at least for me) that the critical aspect/metric is not what Kenji tested – i.e. not the surface one cracks on - but the intensity of your impact. I will expound on this only because Kenji is so great at his chosen mission; I learn a great deal from his books and videos but… I found that the key aspect was not to hit too hard, not to launch sharp shell into the interior of the egg.
Hit just hard enough to get a divot/dimple in the shell large enough to get one’s thumbs in place to further separate the shell halves. Keep the keratin of the outer and inner membranes somewhat intact to enlist their help to catch/keep eggshell fragments from entering the inner vitelline membrane and protecting the yolk. A surprising observation on this is... that more-often brown eggs are easier to break without getting bit of shell into the interior and the impact breaking the yolk.
And while we are on the topic: there are differences between most brown egg varieties and most white shelled eggs (there are many varieties with distinct characteristics) mostly in how well brown vs. white eggs keep over time. Egg shells as well as their outer and inner membranes beneath are breathable. This is how in a fertilized egg a developing chick exchanges carbon dioxide for oxygen. Unfertilized brown eggs stay fresh longer because they have thicker and stronger membranes just under the shell, slower to let in oxygen and let out water when stored. These natural processes over time degrade egg white into a waterier consistency and overall taste of an egg. I tested this by weighing a dozen brown and a dozen white shelled eggs once a week over 60 days. As well as breaking one of each once a week over that time to observe the qualities of the whites and yolk, cooking, and tasting. The results were clear and compelling. If you go through (and repurchase) eggs often then NBD; but if you tend to keep purchased eggs longer in the fridge - then you may want to consider spending a bit more for brown eggs as they keep longer. This is also a good reason to become an egg carton “date-checker” at the store. I have never been able to taste a difference between fresh brown and white shelled eggs; other factors seem to affect taste but not shell color alone.

I've settled on a method that is actually between these two: not the bowl or pan edge because it is often too sharp (also some bowls may tip over upon first strike), and not on a flat surface because the impact area is too wide causing not only the shell to splinter and sometimes explosively so, but also causes trauma to the yolk (the sudden jolting impact will often tear both the yolk sack itself and the surrounding more cohesive part of the egg white). So, I have found that any nearby rounded edge, like a feature of the range or the sink, works best. The key is to strike with just enough force to not only crack the shell but also ever so slightly break the first inner layer. This prevents the egg exploding and leaking all over the place and gives you a crack to gently pull apart the shell over the bowl or pan or whatever. Also, I am very finicky about cleanliness and not getting egg all over the place and on my hands and I have found this method, while not perfect, stays relatively clean. There's two variables NOBODY talks about which is causing all the confusion because not all eggs are created equal: 
1. The thickness of the shell
2. The integrity of the inner membrane separating the shell from the white

Both of those things can be affected by the freshness of the egg, the health of the chickens, what diet they are raised on, etc. Both of those things greatly affect the efficacy of different cracking methodologies. 

I would assume that eggs with a weaker shell and membrane fare worse when cracking on an edge because it's easier to end up with bits of shell in your egg. Conversely, eggs with a stronger shell and membrane fare worse when cracking on a flat surface because the membrane prevents you from getting a clean break, which is what resulted in those two broken yolks you see in the video.

That's why no one can come to a consensus on this. If you wanted to be truly methodical about a test like this, you'd have to use a variety of eggs from different sources.

It minimizes shell bits for two reasons: larger pieces (which you also get from a flat surface), and they're not driven into the shell so much.  It has a benefit over flat cracking in that it's more controlled - you can get a nice straight crack exactly where you want it, which helps minimize yolk breakage.  Also you never need to poke your finger through the membrane like I sometime find myself doing with the flat-crack method.

You should not crack on the side of the bowl because a splinter can fall into the bowl and contaminate your already cracked eggs. You can use the side of another bowl, the side of a thick heavy cutting board, like Kenji's (which are however not common in professional settings), or you can use the side of the table. The problem when you use the side of the table is that you can get the table dirty and it will tend to drip onto the floor and could get the side of your table dirty (in a professional setting you will probably have drawers or cupboards there and you would have to do extra cleaning). You should also always try to crack consciously to apply the right amount of force, avoid a mess and cross-contamination, and recognise and move over the bowl when you have achieved the right crack.

I've definitely bashed a few eggs entirely in half using the edge crack method and then been left with egg dripping down the side of whatever pan/bowl/cup I was using to crack them, meaning I still was left with cleanup (more cleanup than just a towel covered surface where I can remove/wash the towel).

From a material science perspective you need to consider how the shell cracks when pressure is applied different ways both when cracking it and with the tip separating action of the two thumbs. 

Because the surface of the egg is curved cracking it on the flat surface will require the most force, why some of the white leaks out.  

The edge of bowl method requires less force but is more likely to produce small flakes of shell.  

The egg on egg method where two curved surfaces interact with each other )(  is I think the more ideal in terms of force need and shell not flaking off but is better done by striking the egg no on another egg but  something rounded with a 1” - 1-1/2” radius end on it creating a concave * star shaped break pattern with off the three fits the tips of the two thumbs better.  

To test my intuitive hunch based on years of observing how egg shells crack I looked around the kitchen for something with a rounded end I could sit the cutting board and saw and tired a stainless steel expresso tamper which sits flat is heavy, about 3” high — close to bowl rim height — and has a rounded top. The "best" way to crack an eggs depends in part on what you are going to do with the egg.  If it is important to have the yolk intact, then cracking them one by one on the edge of a bowl is probably preferable if you are willing to accept the (low) risk of surface contamination getting into the egg contents.  However, if you are going to be mixing the eggs anyway, and time is important, you can do them more quickly (with a little practice) with one either had hand with less risk of surface contamination by cracking them on a flat surface, and squeezing them from the side, as you did with the first two eggs.
